Fabrication: submitting work (for example, data, evidence or experimental results) which is untrue, made up, falsified or fabricated in any way.
Contract cheating: submitting bought or commissioned work from a third party, including essay mills, other students, friends or family members.
Plagiarism (either intentional or unintentional): using the ideas or work of another person and submitting them as the student’s own.
Cheating in examinations: Using unauthorised materials or methods to complete assignments or exams.
Facilitating the use of unfair means: assisting a fellow student in using any of the forms of academic misconduct defined above, for example in submitting bought or commissioned work.
Impersonation: arranging for someone else to impersonate a student by undertaking their assessment, for example, sitting their examination.
Self-Plagiarism: submitting work that has already been submitted for another assessment, without acknowledgement, or express authorisation by an academic tutor.

Poor academic practice: an inadvertent or low level breach of academic practice arising from a lack of understanding of academic protocols, where there is no evidence of an intention to gain an unfair advantage or to deceive the marker.

process.quote: Such cases must be referred to the Student Conduct and Appeals Team for consideration of a referral to a Summary Hearing or a Senate Discipline Panel in line with University regulations.
Reports of academic misconduct in the assessment process will initially be considered by the relevant academic school who may investigate and respond to the matter.
The process to establish whether a breach has occurred including how they can respond to the allegation and present any information, explanation or mitigating circumstances they feel are relevant.

Matters which are considered serious may be reported to the Chief Operating Officer for consideration for referral to a Summary Hearing or a Senate Discipline Panel in line with university regulations.
The support available to them during and after the process.
The right to appeal and how to do so.
Cases should be concluded within a reasonable timeframe, and not exceeding 30 working days of notification of the suspected breach to the student.

outcomes.quote: Students for whom it is a first breach of academic integrity, at any severity level, must be provided with material and/or tuition to clearly explain why the breach is below the standards expected and guidance as to how correct academic practice can be achieved.
No action beyond a formal warning
Assessment component awarded 0 per cent - no opportunity to resubmit
Assessment component awarded 0 per cent - resubmission required, with no penalty on mark

Module awarded 0 per cent - resit required, but mark capped or reduced, and a compensated pass in the module is not permitted
Expulsion (can only be imposed as a penalty by a Senate Discipline Panel)

definitions.quote: False Authorship wherein authorship is claimed for work that was not solely or substantially created by the individual submitting it.
Automated authorship, involving the inappropriate/unsanctioned use of Artificial Intelligence.
Plagiarism (either intentional or unintentional): using the ideas or work of another person and submitting them as the student’s own.
Self-Plagiarism: submitting work that has already been submitted for another assessment, without acknowledgement, or express authorisation by an academic tutor.
Fabrication: submitting work (for example, data, evidence or experimental results) which is untrue, made up, falsified or fabricated in any way.
Collusion: working with others to produce a piece of work, all or part of which is then submitted by each student as their own individual work without acknowledgement.
Impersonation: arranging for someone else to impersonate a student by undertaking their assessment, for example, sitting their examination.
Contract cheating: submitting bought or commissioned work from a third party, including essay mills, other students, friends or family members.
